title: Two systems, one truth: dual writes and change data capture
goal: By the end, you can tell a copy rebuilt every night from one that follows each change as it happens, show how two writes that both succeed can leave a database and its search copy different for good, and make the copy follow the database's own log without losing, repeating or piling up changes.
opening:
Picture the support desk at a café payments company. A customer calls: her coffee was refunded yesterday, and the refund isn't showing. Support finds the payment: `CAPTURED`. The search screen is a copy, rebuilt every night, so it's a day behind.

The team decides to stop waiting for the night. Whenever a payment changes, the program will update the database and then the search copy at once. Two lines of code, and every test passes. A month later, one payment says `REFUNDED` in the database and `CAPTURED` in search, for good, with no error anywhere.

Two writes that both succeed feel safe: each line is right on its own. The trouble hides between them.

In A lighter log: Redis pub/sub and Streams, a stream wrote every message down and remembered who had taken what. These payments live in a database, so where is their log? In this lesson, we'll watch the two-line version fail in silence, then fix it by having the copy follow the database's own log. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments program writes each status change to the database, and then the same change to the search copy that support uses. Every write returns success, and no error is ever logged. Two requests change payment pay-981 in the same millisecond. What can you say about the search copy afterwards?
options: It matches the database, because both stores got both changes
It may show a different status from the database, for good, with nothing logged
It may be out of date for a moment, and the next change to any payment fixes it
It may be wrong, but the search copy would refuse a change that arrived out of order
warmup.why: Each store applies the changes in the order they reach it, and nothing makes the two orders the same. If the database applies CAPTURED and then REFUNDED, while the search copy applies REFUNDED and then CAPTURED, every write succeeded and the two now disagree until pay-981 changes again. "Out of date for a moment" describes lag: a copy that follows a log falls behind and then catches up. Here no later change is coming to fix it, and a change to some other payment doesn't touch this one. A plain search copy has no idea which change is newer, so it refuses nothing.

sections.h: From a nightly copy to two writes that quietly disagree
sections.body:
Let's look at the program behind that screen. For every card payment, it records which card paid, which shop was paid, how much and when. It keeps each payment as a row in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. A row is one record in a table, like one line of a spreadsheet, and this table is called `payment`.

Each payment has a status: `AUTHORIZED` when the shop has asked your bank to set the money aside, `CAPTURED` once the money really moves, and `REFUNDED` after a refund.

Support staff search a copy built for searching, called a search index. Like the index at the back of a book, it lists each word and where it appears, so a search for refunded payments comes back in milliseconds (thousandths of a second). It lives in OpenSearch, a free program that builds such indexes.

The first version filled the index with a batch job, a program that works through a large, fixed pile of input in one run. Every night at 2:00, it read every payment and rebuilt the index. That's simple, and it's why the customer saw yesterday's status. A café owner who adds up the till receipts after closing works the same way: the totals are right, but only once a day.

The other way is to handle each change as it happens, like a helper who copies each receipt onto a board the moment the till prints it. Data that keeps arriving, with no last item, is called a stream. Each item in it is an event, a record of one thing that happened, such as "pay-981 was refunded at 10:00:02". Working on each event as it arrives is called stream processing. A batch job asks what is in the pile; a stream processor asks what just happened. This track is about the second question.

The team's first stream processor is two lines long. As soon as the database has committed a change, meaning saved it for good, the program sends the same change to the index:

```kotlin
fun setStatus(id: String, status: String) {
    db.update("UPDATE payment SET status = ? WHERE id = ?", status, id)   // committed here
    index.update(id, mapOf("status" to status))                         // then the copy
}
```

Sending one fact to two systems, one after the other, from your own code, is called a **dual write**. It passes every test. Then two requests for `pay-981` arrive within a millisecond. One captures the payment and sets CAPTURED; the other is the shop's refund and sets REFUNDED. Each runs on its own thread, a separate line of work inside the program that runs at the same time as the others. We'll call each one a client. Here is one order they can run in:

| Time | Capture client | Refund client | PostgreSQL | Index |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| t1 | UPDATE to CAPTURED | | CAPTURED | AUTHORIZED |
| t2 | | UPDATE to REFUNDED | REFUNDED | AUTHORIZED |
| t3 | | index to REFUNDED | REFUNDED | REFUNDED |
| t4 | index to CAPTURED | | REFUNDED | CAPTURED |

Every call returned success: no error, no retry, no line in any log. The database says refunded, the index says captured, and it will keep saying so until `pay-981` changes again, which may be never. All it took was a pause of a couple of milliseconds between the capture's two writes, while the program cleared out unused memory, say. Retrying wouldn't help, because both writes succeeded.

Failures open a second door. Say the database write succeeds and the index never answers. Maybe the index made the change and only its reply got lost. Maybe the program crashed between the two lines, and after a restart it doesn't know a second write was owed. Either way, one store has the change and the other doesn't.

Both problems have one root: two systems each decide the order of the writes, and neither follows the other. In the simulator, you play the scheduler, which picks the thread that runs next, and a nightly audit checks the two stores. Find the orders that break it. Then we'll look for a design where the order can't split in two.

sim.title: Two clients, two writes each, two stores
sim.intro: Statuses are numbers here: 0 is AUTHORIZED, 1 CAPTURED, 2 REFUNDED. Each client writes PostgreSQL, then the index. You pick who runs next. Run the audit last. Can you make it report pay-981?

goal.say: PostgreSQL says REFUNDED, the index says CAPTURED. Both clients got success for both writes, nothing threw, nothing was logged. Without this audit, nobody would ever know.

try.title: Count the orders that break it
steps: In the simulator, each client makes two writes, database first. If each client keeps its own order, the four writes can be mixed in 6 ways. Predict how many of the 6 leave PostgreSQL and the index different.
Run all 6 (press Reset between them, and run the audit last each time). Write down `db` and `index` at the end of each run.
try.expect: Two of the six. Capture-db, refund-db, refund-index, capture-index ends with `db = 2` and `index = 1`, and the audit reports it. Refund-db, capture-db, capture-index, refund-index ends with `db = 1` and `index = 2`. This audit misses that one, because it checks only one pattern. In the other four orders, whichever client wrote the database last also wrote the index last. Nothing in the code makes that true. The scheduler makes it true most of the time, which is why the bug survives testing.

refs.title: Kleppmann: Using logs to build a solid data infrastructure (or: why dual writes are a bad idea)

aside.title: Why not run the nightly copy every five minutes?
aside.body: You could, and some teams do. But each run reads every payment, millions of rows that mostly haven't changed, to find the few hundred that did. The copy is still up to five minutes old, and the job slows down as the table grows, until one run doesn't finish before the next one starts. A stream processor does work in proportion to the changes, not to the size of the data. Batch jobs stay the right tool for questions about the whole pile, and the Batch processing and analytics track covers them.

sections.h: One writer decides the order, and the copies follow its log
sections.body:
The first fix people reach for is one transaction across both systems. A transaction is a group of changes that happen all together or not at all. The Transactions track built one that spans machines, in Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA. A coordinator asks each system to prepare, to promise it can commit, then tells each one to commit. That fixes the partial failure. It fixes the race too if both systems keep `pay-981` locked, so that nobody else can change it, until the commit. Count the cost:

1. The index can't take part. OpenSearch, Elasticsearch (the program OpenSearch grew from) and most caches (quick copies kept in memory) have no prepare step, and they don't speak XA, the standard way to run two-phase commit across products.
2. Every payment keeps its row locked while it waits for the index, across the network.
3. Downtime adds up. With PostgreSQL up 99.95% of the time and the index 99.9%, a write that needs both succeeds at most 99.85% of the time. When search is down, nobody can pay.
4. A coordinator that dies halfway leaves the others unsure what to do, holding their locks.

Strike that one. Ask instead why one database never has this problem with its own copies, called replicas. One copy, the leader, takes every write. It decides the order and writes it into a log, and every other copy, a follower, applies the log in that order (the Replication track's first lessons). Two followers that apply the same log in the same order end in the same state.

At the café, only the cashier rings up sales, and the till prints a numbered receipt for each. The helper copies receipts onto the board in number order and notes the last number, so that after a break they can carry on. The till is the leader, the receipts are the log, the helper is a follower, and the note is a bookmark.

Do the same across products. Pick one **system of record**, the store whose data counts as the truth: here, PostgreSQL. The program writes only to it. Every other store becomes a follower: the index, a cache, a warehouse for big reports. Each applies the log of committed changes in order, and keeps a bookmark: the position of the last change it applied.

PostgreSQL already keeps such a log. Before it changes any data, it adds the change to the end of the write-ahead log, or WAL, so that a crash can't lose it. Every place in the WAL has a number called an LSN (log sequence number), written like `0/1C0CC88`, and bigger means later. Each transaction gets a number too, such as 768.

Requests can still race to the database, but now the database settles the race. A transaction takes a row's lock before changing it, and any other transaction that wants the row waits. So the refund waits for the capture, and the result goes into the log once. The index can't disagree about the order, because it no longer picks one. The stepper walks through it.

The price is time. The index hears about each change after the database made it, milliseconds later on a quiet day. A shop that refunds a payment and searches for it at once may not see the refund yet. That delay is called replication lag, and When followers lag: read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix has the fixes.

**Two writers means two orders. Give the data one writer, and let every copy follow its log.**

This needs a log that an outside program can read in order, from wherever it stopped. Next, we'll read PostgreSQL's.

stepper.title: The index follows the database's log
stepper.intro: Two clients race again. This time only PostgreSQL decides the order.

frames.say: Suppose the follower had crashed after applying 769 and before confirming. PostgreSQL would send 768 and 769 again. The restarted follower compares each commit position with its bookmark, finds both at or before `0/1C0CE10`, and skips them. Each change arrives at least once, and the bookmark makes sure it is applied once.

sections.h: Change data capture: reading the log the database already keeps
sections.body:
We don't need to build a new log. Every database keeps one already, to recover from crashes and to feed its replicas. Reading that log from the outside, and turning it into a stream of row changes for other systems, is called **change data capture**, or CDC.

PostgreSQL's WAL records which bytes changed on which page (a fixed-size block) of a file, not which row changed. The Replication track's lesson Replication logs: statements, WAL and logical rows turned it into rows, with a feature called logical decoding. It has three parts:

- The setting `wal_level = logical` makes PostgreSQL write enough detail into the WAL to rebuild each changed row.
- A logical replication slot is PostgreSQL's record of how far one reader has got. While the slot exists, PostgreSQL keeps all the WAL that reader still needs.
- An output plugin turns WAL records into row changes. `test_decoding` prints text a person can read, and `pgoutput` is the compact format that PostgreSQL's own logical replication and Debezium use.

Two properties make this a good log to follow. A transaction comes out only once it has committed, with all its rows together, so one that was rolled back (cancelled) never appears. And transactions come out in commit order, even when they ran at the same time. The Try it shows both on the last section's race: the slot lists 768 (CAPTURED) before 769 (REFUNDED).

Other databases do the same under other names. MySQL, another free database, has its binary log; MongoDB, which stores JSON-like documents instead of rows, has change streams; and DynamoDB, a database Amazon runs for you, has DynamoDB Streams. Go deeper compares them.

Writing a reader for each log is a lot of work, so most teams use **Debezium**, a free program. It has connectors, plug-ins that each read one database's log, for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and other databases such as Oracle, SQL Server and Db2. Each one turns its log into the same shape of change event: the row before, the row after, the kind of change, and its position in the source log. The current stable series is 3.7 (3.7.1.Final).

Debezium usually runs inside Kafka Connect, a program that moves data in and out of Kafka. (Kafka keeps named logs of messages for other programs to read, and the Messaging and logs track built it up.) The next lesson sets Connect up.

Once you do this, your table's columns, the named fields of each row, become something other people's programs read, so renaming one can break a reader you've never met. The next lesson deals with that. But a slot keeps changes only from the moment it was made, so next, we'll give a new follower the rows that came before.

try.title: Race two sessions and read the slot
steps: From the `labs` folder, start only the database from the next lesson's setup file: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml --profile cdc up -d --wait postgres`. Docker runs each program in a container, a sealed-off box on your computer. This command starts PostgreSQL 18 with `wal_level = logical` on port 5433, with an empty `payment` table.

Open psql, PostgreSQL's command-line program for typing SQL: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec postgres psql -U sfz -d payments`. Run the setup block below. It adds two payments and creates a slot named `search_index` that uses `test_decoding`.

Open a second terminal with the same psql command. In terminal 1, run the capture block: it starts a transaction and changes `pay-981` without committing. In terminal 2, run the refund UPDATE. It hangs, waiting for the row's lock. Back in terminal 1, run `COMMIT;` and watch terminal 2 finish.
Predict, then run the last two queries: which status does the table hold, and in which order does the slot list the two transactions?

Time: 1996.387 ms (00:01.996)

---------+------------

    lsn    | xid |  data
-----------+-----+-------------------------------------------------------------------
 0/1C0CC88 | 768 | BEGIN 768
 0/1C0CC88 | 768 | table public.payment: UPDATE: id[text]:'pay-981' account[text]:'acct-17' amount[bigint]:4000 status[text]:'CAPTURED' created_at[...]

(Output trimmed; your LSNs, transaction numbers and wait time differ.) The refund's UPDATE waited about as long as you took to type `COMMIT` in terminal 1: that's the row lock settling the race. The slot lists the capture's transaction and then the refund's, each as BEGIN, its row and COMMIT, in commit order. Each row carries every column, so a follower that applies them in this order ends at REFUNDED, like the table. Peeking shows the changes without using them up. Leave everything running for the next two Try its.

sections.h: Starting a new copy without losing a write
sections.body:
A follower that starts today needs every row, not only today's changes. The WAL doesn't go back to the beginning, because PostgreSQL deletes old WAL once nobody needs it. So a new follower copies the table first, then applies the log after the copy. The hard word is "after": a write that commits while the copy runs must still reach the index.

Get the order wrong, and that write is lost. Copy the table at 10:00:00, create the slot at 10:00:05, and a refund that commits at 10:00:02 is in neither. The copy started before it, and the slot didn't exist yet. The index shows the old status until that payment changes again.

Create the slot first, then copy. From the moment the slot exists, PostgreSQL keeps every committed change for it. So a write during the copy is in the slot for sure, and maybe in the copy too. Getting it twice is harmless, because each change carries the whole row ("pay-981 is REFUNDED, account acct-17, amount 4000"), not "change the status". Writing the same price on the café's board twice leaves the same price. A slot can even hand out a snapshot, a frozen view of the database as the slot begins, so that copy and log meet with no overlap (Go deeper shows how).

Debezium does this on its first start (`snapshot.mode = initial`). It sends every row of each captured table as a read event (`op` is `r`), then follows the slot. One long copy of a 2 TB table takes hours and keeps one transaction open the whole time, which holds up PostgreSQL's cleanup. So Debezium also offers incremental snapshots, built on DBLog, a design from Netflix. It copies the table in small chunks, ordered by primary key (the column that names each row), while the log keeps flowing. Markers in the log around each chunk show which rows changed during it, and those rows come from the log instead. Nothing is locked, and the copy can pause and carry on.

There's one more habit to plan for. PostgreSQL saves a slot's confirmed position only at checkpoints, the moments when it writes changes from memory into the data files and notes how far it got. So after a database crash, the slot may step back and send recent changes again. A follower can also crash after applying a change and before confirming it. Either way, some changes arrive twice. That makes CDC **at-least-once**: every change arrives, and some arrive more than once.

The fix is the stepper's bookmark. Store the commit position of the last transaction you applied with the data, in the same write, and skip anything at or before it. The Try it shows that nothing leaves the slot until the follower confirms it. Next, we'll see what that patience costs when nobody comes back to confirm.

try.title: Nothing leaves the slot until you confirm it
steps: In psql, peek at the slot again. Predict: are the two transactions from the last Try it still there?

Confirm them by moving the slot on to the last COMMIT's LSN with `pg_replication_slot_advance`, which is what a follower does once it has applied them. Peek once more. Then commit one more change and peek again.

-------

That's what a follower sees after crashing before it confirmed, so it must skip what it already applied. Moving the slot to the last COMMIT's LSN told PostgreSQL the follower has everything up to there. The slot then held nothing until the next transaction.

sections.h: A slot nobody reads fills the database's disk
sections.body:
A slot is a promise: PostgreSQL won't delete WAL the reader hasn't confirmed, even if the reader is gone. Picture a connector paused for a long weekend, or a test slot someone forgot. The slot stays, and every write adds WAL that can't be deleted. At the café, the till would keep every receipt the helper hasn't collected. Here the picture breaks. Paper piling up is untidy, but a full disk stops the database.

Gunnar Morling, one of Debezium's developers, described the case that surprises people. An inactive Debezium slot on Amazon RDS, Amazon's service that runs PostgreSQL for you, filled a 200 GiB disk in under two weeks. That's about 18 GB a day, and the tables it captured weren't changing at all.

The WAL came from RDS itself. Every 5 minutes, RDS writes a tiny "still alive" record, a heartbeat, into its own internal database (`rdsadmin`). A setting called `archive_timeout` then makes PostgreSQL start a new WAL file, called a segment, and RDS segments are 64 MB. The slot holds every one: 64 MB × 12 an hour × 24 hours is about 18 GB a day. When the WAL folder (`pg_wal`) is full, the server stops, and every payment stops with it.

A slot also holds back VACUUM, PostgreSQL's cleanup process, on its internal tables. In extreme cases, PostgreSQL shuts down rather than run out of transaction numbers. So run a slot like part of the database, because it is:

1. Measure it. The WAL a slot keeps is `pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)` from `pg_replication_slots`: where the WAL is now, minus the oldest point the slot needs. Alert above a limit you choose (Morling suggests starting around 100 MB), and when `active` has been false for long.
2. Keep quiet slots moving. Debezium's heartbeat, or an occasional `SELECT pg_logical_emit_message(false, 'heartbeat', now()::text)`, writes a tiny change that the connector reads and confirms. Then the slot moves even when the tables are idle. `pgoutput` carries these messages since PostgreSQL 14.
3. Cap it. `max_slot_wal_keep_size` (default -1, no limit) lets PostgreSQL give up on a slot that falls too far behind. PostgreSQL 18's `idle_replication_slot_timeout` gives up on slots unused for too long (default 0, off). Both swap a full disk for a broken slot, and the follower then needs a new snapshot.
4. Drop slots you no longer need.

The Try it watches an unread slot keep tens of megabytes after 200,000 inserts.

That's where today's design stops. The follower is correct, but we wrote all of it by hand, for one table and one index. And every reader sees our table's columns exactly as they are. Next, we'll hand the follower to Kafka Connect and Debezium, and give the readers events we design on purpose.

try.title: Watch an unread slot hold WAL
steps: In psql, insert 200,000 rows while nobody reads the slot. Then look at how much WAL the slot holds: `unconfirmed` is what the reader hasn't confirmed, and `retained` is what PostgreSQL must keep on disk for it.

Move the slot on, as a reader that caught up would, then run `CHECKPOINT` and move it once more. PostgreSQL moves the slot's `restart_lsn` only to a point where it has written down which transactions were running, and a checkpoint writes that down. Look again.
Clean up: `SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('search_index');`, then from the `labs` folder `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml --profile cdc down -v`.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
```text
INSERT 0 200000
  slot_name   | active | wal_status | unconfirmed | retained
--------------+--------+------------+-------------+----------
 search_index | f      | reserved   | 58 MB       | 58 MB

  slot_name   |  end_lsn
--------------+-----------
 search_index | 0/9B545F0
CHECKPOINT
  slot_name   |  end_lsn
--------------+-----------
 search_index | 0/9B546C0

  slot_name   | active | wal_status | unconfirmed | retained
--------------+--------+------------+-------------+-----------
 search_index | f      | reserved   | 0 bytes     | 176 bytes
```
(Output trimmed; the retained size varies between runs, about 40 to 60 MB here, depending on what the last checkpoint left.) The slot has no reader (`active` is f) and holds every byte of WAL written since its position: 200,000 small rows cost tens of megabytes, and an idle RDS database's heartbeats cost about 18 GB a day. Once the slot moved past a checkpoint's record of running transactions, the kept WAL dropped to a few hundred bytes. `wal_status = reserved` means nothing caps it, because `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is -1 by default.

compare.title: A dual write, and the same change through a follower

a.label: Dual write
a.title: the program writes both stores

b.label: Follower of the log
b.title: the program writes PostgreSQL; a follower writes the index

compare.note: On the left, two writers each pick an order, and nothing ties them together, so the stores can disagree with no error. On the right, PostgreSQL is the only writer that picks an order, and the follower replays that order. The follower adds two things the dual write never had: a position in a log, so it can stop and carry on, and a rule for repeats, which skips anything at or before the bookmark. What it gives up is freshness: the index trails the table by however long the follower takes.

worked.title: Turn a refund program's dual write into a follower

steps.say: Find the dual write. The refund handler, the code that runs for each refund, saves the refund to PostgreSQL and then sends it to OpenSearch. That's two writers and two orders, and a crash between the lines loses the index write.
steps.code:
refundRepository.save(refund)                       // PostgreSQL, committed
searchClient.index("refunds", refund.id, refund.toDoc())   // OpenSearch, a separate system

steps.say: Delete the second line. The handler now writes only to PostgreSQL, the system of record. Nothing else in it changes.

Give the new follower its first copy without losing a write: create the slot first, then copy the table. Anything committed in between is in both, which is harmless because each change carries the whole row.
Follow the slot. Apply each committed transaction once, in commit order, and keep the bookmark with the index. Confirm only after applying, so a crash costs a replay, never a lost change.

Watch the slot from the first day. Alert when it keeps more than about 100 MB of WAL or has had no reader for a while, and set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` so that the worst case is a new copy, not a full disk.
steps.code:
SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots
WHERE pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) > 100 * 1024 * 1024;

lab.title: Race a dual write, then make the index follow the log
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 11 fail. They start one PostgreSQL 18 container with `wal_level = logical`, shared by every test of this lesson, holding the `payment` table. `Given.kt` has the `SearchIndex` (an in-memory stand-in for OpenSearch), the `Slot` helpers (create, peek, confirm, lag) and a reader for `test_decoding` lines.

In `DualWrite.kt`, write `race`. Run the capture and refund clients on two threads, and use two `CountDownLatch`es so that the writes happen in the order the comment above `race` lists. (A `CountDownLatch` is a Java object that makes one thread wait until another counts it down to zero.) The test checks that the database says REFUNDED, the index says CAPTURED, and nothing threw an error.

In `ChangeFollower.kt`, write `poll`. Peek at the slot and collect the `public.payment` rows between each BEGIN and COMMIT. Apply a transaction only if its COMMIT LSN is after `index.appliedLsn`, mark it applied, and confirm the last COMMIT LSN at the end.

Write `bootstrap`: create the slot, call the hook, then copy the table with one SELECT. Run the tests until all 11 pass. The test that calls `poll(confirm = false)` plays a crash between applying and confirming.
hints: In `race`, the capture client calls `setStatus` with a `between` function that counts down the first latch and then waits on the second. The refund client waits on the first latch, calls `setStatus`, then counts down the second.
`TestDecoding.parse(change.data)` returns `Decoded.Begin`, `Decoded.Row` or `Decoded.Commit`. The COMMIT entry's `change.lsn` is the transaction's position.
Build a payment from a row with `Payment(c.getValue("id")!!, c.getValue("account")!!, c.getValue("amount")!!.toLong(), c.getValue("status")!!)`. A DELETE row carries only `id`.

drill.title: The follower loop from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, a follower's `poll()` over a slot that returns BEGIN, row and COMMIT entries in commit order. It must apply each committed transaction once, even if the slot sends some of them again, and it must never lose a change if it crashes. Then answer: should it confirm before applying, or after?

recap: A batch job rebuilds a copy from the whole pile now and then. Stream processing handles each event, one thing that happened, as it arrives, so copies stay fresh. This track is about doing that correctly.

A dual write (the database, then the index, from your own code) has two writers that each pick an order. Two racing requests can leave the stores different for good, with every call successful and nothing logged, and a crash between the writes loses one.
Two-phase commit could tie the writes together, but the index can't take part, every write waits for both systems, and an index outage stops payments.

Make one system of record the leader and let every other store follow its log of committed changes, in order, with a bookmark. Change data capture reads that log: PostgreSQL's WAL through a logical slot, MySQL's binary log, MongoDB change streams, DynamoDB Streams. Debezium 3.7 gives them one shape.
A new follower creates its slot first and copies the table second. Changes can arrive twice, so it skips anything at or before its bookmark.

The limit: a slot nobody reads keeps WAL until the disk fills (about 18 GB a day on an idle RDS database). Alert on kept WAL, send heartbeats, set `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, and drop slots you don't use.
closing:
We started with a support screen that said `CAPTURED` for a refunded coffee: first because it was rebuilt every night, then because two writes raced. The fix was one writer, the database, and a copy that follows its log in order, with a bookmark and a slot someone watches.

If you can reach a PostgreSQL database, run `SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn FROM pg_replication_slots;`. Every row is a reader that PostgreSQL is keeping WAL for, and a row with `active` false is one nobody is reading right now.

Next, we'll hand the follower to Kafka Connect and Debezium, and ask what happens to every reader when someone renames a column.

quiz.q: Which of these is a dual write?
options: Inserting a payment row and an event row in the same PostgreSQL transaction
Updating the payment row, then sending the new status to Kafka with `producer.send`
Debezium reading the payment table's changes from the WAL
A PostgreSQL replica replaying the leader's WAL
quiz.why: Two writes to two systems, one after the other, with nothing tying them together: the database and Kafka (a program that keeps logs of messages) can see racing updates in different orders, and a crash between the two loses the send. Two rows in one transaction are one write to one system. Debezium and the replica both follow a single log, which is the fix.

quiz.q: Someone proposes two-phase commit, using XA, across PostgreSQL and the search index to fix the race. What's the strongest objection?
options: XA can't make two writes happen all together or not at all
XA would order the writes by each machine's clock, and clocks drift apart
The search index has no prepare step, and even if it had one, every payment write would wait for the index and fail when it's down
XA only works inside one database
quiz.why: Two-phase commit does make writes happen together, and with locks held to the end it would even settle the race. But OpenSearch, Elasticsearch and caches can't take part in XA. If they could, each write would hold its lock while waiting for the index and fail whenever the index is down. XA is built for several products, and it orders nothing by clocks.

quiz.q: From Replication logs: statements, WAL and logical rows. A follower crashes after applying a decoded UPDATE and gets it again when it restarts. Why is applying `status[text]:'REFUNDED' amount[bigint]:4000` twice harmless, when running `UPDATE ... SET amount = amount + 50` twice is not?
options: PostgreSQL throws away the second delivery for you
The decoded entry carries the row's resulting values, so applying it again sets the same values
Decoded entries are sent only once, so it can't happen
The search index refuses a document it has already seen
quiz.why: A row-level log records results, not the statement that produced them, so applying an entry twice leaves the row the same. A statement like `amount + 50` changes the value each time it runs. PostgreSQL really does send again after a crash, because a slot's position is saved only at checkpoints, and nothing in the index removes repeats for you. That's what the bookmark is for.

quiz.q: You build a new index. You copy the `payment` table at 10:00:00 and create the slot at 10:00:05. A refund commits at 10:00:02. Where is the refund?
options: In the copy, because the copy took a while
In the slot, because a slot starts from the oldest WAL
In both, which is harmless
In neither: the index shows the old status until that payment changes again
quiz.why: The copy saw the database as it was before the refund committed, and the slot keeps only changes committed after it was created. Create the slot first and copy second. Then a change in between is in the slot for sure, and maybe in the copy too, which is harmless because each change carries the whole row.

quiz.q: A Debezium connector on an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database is stopped for 10 days. The tables it captures get no writes at all. What happens on the database?
options: Nothing: no writes means no new WAL for the slot to keep
The slot is dropped automatically after 24 hours
WAL keeps piling up from RDS's own heartbeat writes, about 18 GB a day, because the slot keeps every segment
PostgreSQL pauses the slot and frees its WAL until the connector returns
quiz.why: RDS writes a heartbeat every 5 minutes and starts a new 64 MB WAL segment, and the slot keeps all of them: about 180 GB in 10 days. `max_slot_wal_keep_size` is -1 (no limit) and `idle_replication_slot_timeout` is 0 (off) by default, so nothing drops or gives up on the slot unless you set it up. Heartbeats that the connector reads and confirms keep the slot moving.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a batch job and stream processing?
flashcards.back: A batch job works through a fixed pile of data in one run, say every night. Stream processing handles each event as it arrives, so its results are seconds old, not a day.
Your program writes the same fact to two systems, one after the other, such as PostgreSQL and then a search index. Racing requests can leave them different, and a crash between the writes loses one.

flashcards.front: Why can a dual-write race leave the stores different with no error?
flashcards.back: Each store applies writes in the order they arrive, and the two orders can differ. Every write succeeds, and the stores end with different last writers.

flashcards.front: What does change data capture do?
flashcards.back: It reads the database's own log of committed changes and turns it into a stream of row changes, in commit order, for other systems to follow.

flashcards.front: A new follower: slot first or copy first?
flashcards.back: Slot first, then copy. A change committed in between is in the slot, and maybe in the copy too, which is harmless because each change carries the whole row.

flashcards.front: Why does CDC send some changes twice, and what handles it?
flashcards.back: PostgreSQL saves a slot's position only at checkpoints, and a follower can crash before confirming. Store the last applied commit LSN with the data and skip anything at or before it.

flashcards.front: What happens to the WAL held by a slot nobody reads?
flashcards.back: PostgreSQL keeps it until the disk fills (by default `max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1`, no limit). Alert on kept WAL, send heartbeats, set a cap, drop unused slots.

terms.plain: Handling each event, a record of one thing that happened, as it arrives, instead of working through a stored pile in one run.
Your program writing the same change to two systems, one after the other, with nothing tying the two writes together.
The one store whose data counts as the truth; every other copy is worked out from it.
Reading a database's log of committed changes and turning it into a stream that other systems apply.
PostgreSQL's log on disk: every change is added to it before the data files change, so a crash loses nothing.
PostgreSQL's record of how far one reader has read the decoded WAL. It keeps the WAL until the reader confirms it.
Log sequence number: a position in PostgreSQL's WAL, written like 0/1C0CD30. Bigger means later.
The first full copy a new follower takes of the data, lined up with a log position so that the changes after it can be applied.

explain_back.prompt: A friend's program updates PostgreSQL and then the search index, and retries whenever a call fails. Explain how the index can end up wrong for good with no error, why two-phase commit is the wrong fix, what you'd do instead, and the one thing you'd watch.
explain_back.answer: Each store applies writes in the order they reach it. If two requests change the same payment at once, PostgreSQL can apply A then B while the index applies B then A, because one request paused between its two writes. Every call succeeds, so the retries never run, and the index keeps the wrong value until that payment changes again. A crash between the two writes is a second way to lose one of them. Two-phase commit would tie the writes together, but the index can't take part in it, each write would wait for both systems, and an index outage would stop payments. Instead, make PostgreSQL the only writer and the index a follower. It reads the committed changes from a logical replication slot, applies them in commit order, and keeps the last applied commit LSN next to the index, so that repeats after a crash are skipped. A new index starts by creating the slot first and then copying the table. And watch the slot's kept WAL, because a slot nobody reads keeps WAL until the database's disk is full.

deeper.body:
**Snapshots that match the slot exactly.** A slot can also be made over the replication protocol, the special connection that replicas use. `CREATE_REPLICATION_SLOT name LOGICAL pgoutput (SNAPSHOT 'export')` returns a snapshot name along with the slot. A second session runs `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SET TRANSACTION SNAPSHOT '<name>';` and copies the tables. It sees the database exactly as of the slot's start, so not even a harmless overlap remains. The exported snapshot lasts only until the session that made it runs its next command.

**DBLog's markers.** For each chunk, DBLog writes a low watermark, a marker, into the log, selects the chunk by primary key, then writes a high watermark. While the log between the two markers streams past, any key that changed in that window is removed from the chunk's result, and the rest of the chunk is sent at the high watermark. The log's version of a row always wins over the copy's, and nothing is locked.

**The same idea in other databases.** Each database's log has its own name, its own bookmark and its own trap:

| Database | Its log of changes | A reader's place | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL 18 | the WAL, through a logical slot | an LSN | a slot nobody reads keeps WAL forever (the lesson's last section) |
| MySQL 8.4 | the binary log, recording whole rows (`binlog_format = ROW`, `binlog_row_image = FULL`) | a binlog file and position | deleted after 30 days by default (`binlog_expire_logs_seconds`), even if a reader is behind |
| MongoDB 9.0 | change streams, on a replica set (a group of copies) or a sharded cluster (data split across machines) | a resume token | shows only changes most copies have saved; the `updateLookup` option gives the document as it is *now* |
| DynamoDB | DynamoDB Streams | a sequence number per shard | records last 24 hours; order holds per item, not per table |

**MySQL positions.** Besides a binlog file name and position, a MySQL reader can keep its place as a GTID set: the global transaction ids it has seen. Unlike a file position, that still makes sense after another server takes over as the leader.

**Failover.** A logical slot lives on the leader. If the leader fails and a follower takes over, a slot that didn't exist on that follower is gone, and the reader needs a new snapshot. PostgreSQL 18's documentation describes failover slots: create the slot with `failover = true` and set `sync_replication_slots` on the standby (the follower that would take over), and the standby keeps a synchronized copy of the slot.

**Debezium Server.** Debezium can also run on its own, without Kafka Connect, and send its change events to other systems.

**Databases with no leader.** Cassandra writes each row to several machines with no single leader, so it has no single log to follow. Each node writes its own commit log, its CDC hands out per-node pieces, and a reader has to merge them and drop the repeats that copying creates.

**An outbox without a table.** `pg_logical_emit_message(true, 'payments', '{...}')` writes a message into the WAL inside your transaction, and decoding hands it out at commit with the transaction's rows. It's an event with no table to grow, a variant of the next lesson's outbox.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, covers the same ground under "Databases and Streams".
